messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Three years ago, Thomas was attending a professional summit at the Grandview Convention Center when a deliberate electrical fire tore through the east wing. What began as a flicker rapidly became a wall of black smoke that swallowed the corridors. In the chaos, panicked attendees began hurling heavy chairs and luggage out of emergency exits to clear escape routes, the heavy thuds and sharp impacts echoing through the stairwells. Thomas found himself trapped on a landing, his lungs burning as he inhaled thick, acrid plumes of burning insulation and melting plastic. He had to push through the smoke, his vision blurring, until he finally stumbled onto the pavement, gasping. The disaster left him physically unscathed but psychologically unmoored. In the weeks that followed, the sharp tang of burnt toast from a neighbor’s kitchen would freeze him in his own hallway, and watching a delivery driver casually toss a heavy package onto a porch would send his heart hammering against his ribs. These ordinary moments of sudden motion and acrid air did not simply startle him; they pulled the terror of the convention center back into his body. Rather than sit with the rising panic, Thomas immediately excused himself, retreating into isolation and shutting down any attempt to process the event. He told himself that allowing his mind to drift toward the tragedy would fracture his composure entirely, so he began systematically declining invitations from friends and refusing to engage with any shared narratives about the past. These encounters did not conjure clear pictures, but rather delivered the full, suffocating panic of that stairwell without any contextual image. Because Thomas had come to believe his own body was a liability and that mental lapses would trigger an irrecoverable breakdown, he kept the recollection locked in that detached, sensory state, never allowing it to settle into a coherent timeline. He would look at his own reflection and feel as though the terrified man in the smoke belonged to a stranger. That unprocessed, image-less recall convinced him that his nervous system was betraying him, reinforcing the conviction that he must stay hyper-alert to the next threat if he was to survive it. He now spent his days in his private counseling office, deliberately sitting with his back to the door, his posture rigid, scanning the room for any hint of smoke or sudden movement. He monitored his own internal dialogue with exhausting precision, scanning for any drift toward the event, convinced that even a momentary lapse in mental control would be catastrophic. Over months, the cycle tightened. By systematically avoiding friends and enforcing rigid thought suppression, he starved the recollection of any chance for integration, ensuring it remained trapped in that alien, unplaceable loop. His unrelenting alertness made every ordinary occurrence—a dropped pen, a whistling kettle—feel like a precursor to catastrophe. The more the memory solidified as an unplaceable terror, the more powerfully those same smells and sudden motions felt like imminent disaster, dragging the raw fear back into his awareness the moment they surfaced. Thomas realized he was no longer living in the present; he was managing a perpetual emergency. He had come to believe that the only way to stay safe was to keep his thoughts locked away and his world tightly controlled. Yet the control was fraying. He finally sought help not because the fear had lessened, but because the exhaustion of monitoring his own mind, of flinching at every discarded object and lingering scent, had left him unable to continue practicing therapy or maintaining even the bare minimum of his daily routine. He sits now in a clinician’s office, hoping to learn how to quiet the alarm system that refuses to turn off, afraid that if he stops watching for danger, he will be swallowed by it all over again.
